A.explanation: Driving force is $2000 - mg\sin6.0^{\circ} \approx 460\text{ N}$ down the slope, so $P = Fv \approx 460 \times 30 \approx 14\text{ kW}$.

B.explanation: This is $2000\text{ N} \times 30\text{ m s}^{-1} = 60\text{ kW}$, which ignores the downhill component of weight that assists the motion.

C.explanation: This adds the weight component to the resistive force instead of subtracting it, as if the car were travelling uphill.

D.explanation: This is of order $mgv$, using the full weight rather than the small $mg\sin6.0^{\circ}$ component along the $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ direction.

hints: Notice the car moves at constant velocity down the $6.0^{\circ}$ slope, so forces along the slope must balance to zero with the $2000\text{ N}$ resistive force acting up the slope.
Resolve the weight $1500\text{ kg}$ into a component along the slope: $mg\sin6.0^{\circ}$ acting down the slope and assisting the engine.
Use $P = Fv$ with $v = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$, where $F$ is only the engine driving force needed to make up the difference between $2000\text{ N}$ and the downhill weight component.
walkthrough: Constant velocity means resultant force along the slope is zero. Take down the slope as positive: driving force $F$ from engine plus downhill weight component minus $2000\text{ N}$ resistive force up the slope equals zero.
Calculate the downhill component of weight: $W_{parallel} = mg\sin\theta = 1500 \times 9.81 \times \sin6.0^{\circ}$.
Force balance gives $F + 1540 - 2000 = 0$, so $F = 2000 - 1540 \approx 460\text{ N}$ down the slope. The engine still pushes forward because resistance exceeds the gravitational pull.
Power output is $P = Fv$ for force parallel to velocity: $P \approx 460 \times 30 = 13800\text{ W} \approx 14\text{ kW}$. This is option A.
